transformation. Once equated with relentless output and longer working hours, productivity is

questions.stimulus:
I.	There are, in every workplace, two kinds of people. The first category consists of those who, either
as a function of dedication or neurotic tendencies, check every email, answer every text and
respond with an almost annoying alacrity on the office WhatsApp group. These front-benchers are,
unsurprisingly, the blue-eyed boys and girls of upper management. More often than not, though,
they are relative outliers. The majority of the bell curve has scores of unread emails, will often
have to be reminded to check their messages and will, much to the chagrin of the powers that be,
treat the job as work that ends with the workday. It is this second category that is causing a
headache for the Delhi government.
Over the last three months, the Delhi government’s IT department has been trying to nudge
bureaucrats — including at the secretary level — to read their official emails. It seems that
despite the repeated advisories and notices, officials do not regularly log in. This is a major
problem, not least because official instructions and notices are sent to the official address. (This
begs the question of whether the notice to check the official email was sent on the official email.)
Their official email is also linked to the portals of several government portals and services. If it is
not checked for three months, the officers lose access to all that it provides.
There is no easy answer to the problem that plagues the government of Delhi. Bureaucrats, like so
many people today, are inundated — on social media, personal WhatsApp groups, etc. But then, in
every workplace, there is a price to be paid for not being up to speed — a nagging boss, an
annoying HR missive. With every unread mail, the offending officer must ask herself: Is avoiding a
bit of boredom worth the hassle, really?

annoying HR missive. With every unread mail, the offending officer must ask herself: Is avoiding a

Til. When the town of Velmora first learned of the bridge, it did not celebrate. Bridges, the elders
insisted, were instruments of impatience. For generations, the river Arven had served not merely
as a boundary but as a tutor, instructing the townspeople in the virtues of waiting. Traders timed
their journeys to its moods; children learned early that certain crossings belonged only to certain
seasons. To conquer the river with steel seemed, to many, an act bordering on insolence.
Yet the council approved the project with unusual haste. Velmora, once peripheral and self-
contained, had begun to feel the gravitational pull of distant cities. Younger merchants
complained that the ferry rendered commerce whimsical and reputations fragile. A missed
crossing could undo months of negotiation. Efficiency, they argued, was not impatience but
survival.
Construction commenced amid a silence more unsettling than protest. The engineer, a soft-spoken
outsider named Ilyen, soon became an object of wary curiosity. He neither defended nor
disparaged the bridge; he spoke instead of load distributions and tolerances, of how structures,
like arguments, fail at their weakest points. His metaphors, though polite, irritated the elders,
who suspected that calculation was merely arrogance in numerical dress.
As pylons rose from the riverbed, subtle transformations unsettled the town. The ferry operators,
once indispensable, found themselves treated with an awkward courtesy usually reserved for the
convalescent. Children, sensing history’s pivot, abandoned old games for speculation about the
traffic the bridge would invite. Even the elders grew restless, their criticisms acquiring an urgency
that belied their professed allegiance to patience.www.lawpreptutorial.com
On the morning the bridge opened, Velmora gathered without ceremony. No speeches were made.
The first crossing fell, unexpectedly, to Mara, the eldest ferrywoman, whose livelihood the bridge
had rendered obsolete. She stepped onto the span with neither defiance nor nostalgia, pausing
midway as if to consult the river one last time. Observers later disagreed about her expression:
some detected sorrow, others relief, a few something closer to amusement.
By evening, the bridge had already begun its quiet work of rearrangement. Strangers entered.
Departures multiplied. Transactions accelerated. And the river, indifferent yet altered, flowed
beneath a structure that promised permanence while whispering, to those inclined to listen, of
stresses accumulating beyond sight.

questions.stimulus:
IV.	By the time the notice appeared on the college board, the banyan tree had already begun to shed.
Its leaves fell with an unhurried confidence, collecting along the stone path where students paused
between lectures. Few read the announcement fully; most registered only its headline —
Redevelopment Proposal Approved.
The tree stood at the centre of the courtyard, older than any building that now framed it.
Professors referenced it absentmindedly when giving directions, as though it were a structural
necessity rather than an organism. Alumni recalled it with a proprietary fondness, attributing to
its shade friendships, epiphanies, and occasionally academic redemption. Yet its presence had long
ago dissolved into familiarity, the kind that escapes notice precisely because it endures.
The administration’s reasoning was impeccably rational. The courtyard, they explained, occupied
valuable space that could accommodate a research wing and expanded facilities. Progress
demanded optimisation; sentiment, while understandable, could not obstruct institutional growth.
The proposal included assurances: new landscaping, commemorative plaques, even a digital
archive preserving the tree’s “legacy.”
Reactions emerged in curious forms. A few students organised petitions whose urgency wavered
between examinations and internships. Others treated the news with ironic detachment,
photographing the tree with captions that rehearsed nostalgia before loss had actually occurred.
Faculty debates grew unexpectedly philosophical, drifting from budgetary constraints to
abstractions about heritage and utility.
Only the groundskeeper, Raman, seemed untouched by deliberation. For decades he had tended
the courtyard with an attentiveness bordering on ritual, sweeping its paths before dawn and
watering the tree during summers of reluctant rain. When asked about the redevelopment, he
responded with a politeness that resisted interpretation. “Institutions,” he said once, “have longer
memories than people, but shorter patience.”
The day the workers arrived, the campus adopted a strained normalcy. Lectures proceeded.
Conversations persisted. Yet attention gravitated toward the courtyard, where the machinery

waited with an air of procedural inevitability. Raman stood nearby, neither obstructing nor
assisting, his expression unreadable.
The first cut produced no dramatic spectacle — only a sound oddly disproportionate to the act, as
though something abstract had been disturbed. Students who had never consciously valued the
tree now lingered at windows. Silence accumulated, tentative yet pervasive.
In the weeks that followed, the courtyard transformed efficiently. Concrete replaced roots. Glass
replaced shade. The new wing rose with admirable speed, celebrated in newsletters and brochures.
Life resumed its rhythms, apparently undiminished. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Yet certain absences proved resistant to articulation. Directions required revision. Gatherings
dispersed more quickly under the unmediated sun. And Raman, sweeping the newly paved
expanse each morning, found little to collect except dust, which, unlike leaves, offered no evidence
of having once belonged.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. The Supreme Court of India has established stringent safeguards for convictions based on
circumstantial evidence, where no direct eyewitness testimony exists and guilt must be inferred
from surrounding facts. In the landmark judgment of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of
Maharashtra, the Court articulated the "Five Golden Principles" or "Panchsheel of Circumstantial
Evidence": (1) circumstances must be fully established, (2) they must be consistent only with the
guilt of the accused, (3) they must be conclusive in nature and tendency, (4) they must exclude
every possible hypothesis except guilt, and (5) there must be a complete chain of evidence with no
missing links. These principles mandate extreme judicial caution because conviction relies on
inference rather than direct observation, creating possibilities for human error, conjecture, and
suspicion masquerading as proof. The First Information Report (FIR), though not substantive
evidence, plays a crucial evidentiary role. Under Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
omissions of important facts in the FIR are relevant in judging witness veracity, as recognized in
Ram Kumar Pandey v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Omissions become particularly serious when
known accused names are absent, crucial facts appear only in later statements, or the FIR
contradicts the prosecution's subsequent narrative. In circumstantial cases, such omissions
significantly weaken the evidentiary chain. Test Identification Parades (TIP), conducted before a
Magistrate during investigation, serve to test a witness's memory and identification capacity. As
clarified in P. Sasikumar v. State, while TIP itself is not substantive evidence, dock identification

in court constitutes substantive evidence. However, when the accused is a stranger to the witness
and no TIP was conducted, dock identification becomes inherently unsafe due to memory
degradation, possible police exposure influencing recognition, and the suggestive nature of
courtroom settings. The "last seen theory" whereby guilt may be inferred if accused and deceased
were last seen together shortly before death requires extreme caution. In State of U.P. v. Satish,
the Court held that the time gap must be so minimal that third-party intervention is effectively
ruled out. This principle was consistently reiterated in Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana, Chattar
Singh v. State of Haryana, and Krishan Kumar v. State of Haryana, where the Court emphasized
that last seen evidence alone is insufficient, requires corroboration, and cannot be stretched
through conjecture or across wide time gaps. Scientific evidence including DNA analysis,
fingerprints, Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) reports, serology, and ballistics provides objective,
independent verification less prone to human bias. When scientific evidence is neutral or
exculpatory such as DNA mismatches, blood group inconsistencies, or failure to link weapons,
courts cannot ignore these findings and convict on suspicion alone. The fundamental principle,
articulated in Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, mandates that when two views are possible
one indicating guilt and another innocence the accused must receive the benefit of doubt.
Suspicion, regardless of strength, cannot substitute proof beyond reasonable doubt, which remains
the immutable standard in criminal law.

options.text:
Conviction is unsustainable because dock identification without a prior TIP is inherently
unsafe under the P. Sasikumar rule regardless of other corroborative evidence.

options.label: b
options.text:
Conviction is sustainable because the 20-minute gap satisfies the last seen theory, fingerprints
are scientific evidence, and TIP is only required for strangers.

options.label: c
options.text:
Conviction is unsustainable because the last seen theory requires independent corroboration
and cannot stand alone as the sole basis for conviction in this case.

options.label: d

Conviction is sustainable because fingerprints constitute conclusive scientific evidence which
legally overrides any procedural defects regarding the witness identification.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. The Supreme Court of India has established stringent safeguards for convictions based on
circumstantial evidence, where no direct eyewitness testimony exists and guilt must be inferred
from surrounding facts. In the landmark judgment of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of
Maharashtra, the Court articulated the "Five Golden Principles" or "Panchsheel of Circumstantial
Evidence": (1) circumstances must be fully established, (2) they must be consistent only with the
guilt of the accused, (3) they must be conclusive in nature and tendency, (4) they must exclude
every possible hypothesis except guilt, and (5) there must be a complete chain of evidence with no
missing links. These principles mandate extreme judicial caution because conviction relies on
inference rather than direct observation, creating possibilities for human error, conjecture, and
suspicion masquerading as proof. The First Information Report (FIR), though not substantive
evidence, plays a crucial evidentiary role. Under Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
omissions of important facts in the FIR are relevant in judging witness veracity, as recognized in
Ram Kumar Pandey v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Omissions become particularly serious when
known accused names are absent, crucial facts appear only in later statements, or the FIR
contradicts the prosecution's subsequent narrative. In circumstantial cases, such omissions
significantly weaken the evidentiary chain. Test Identification Parades (TIP), conducted before a
Magistrate during investigation, serve to test a witness's memory and identification capacity. As
clarified in P. Sasikumar v. State, while TIP itself is not substantive evidence, dock identification

in court constitutes substantive evidence. However, when the accused is a stranger to the witness
and no TIP was conducted, dock identification becomes inherently unsafe due to memory
degradation, possible police exposure influencing recognition, and the suggestive nature of
courtroom settings. The "last seen theory" whereby guilt may be inferred if accused and deceased
were last seen together shortly before death requires extreme caution. In State of U.P. v. Satish,
the Court held that the time gap must be so minimal that third-party intervention is effectively
ruled out. This principle was consistently reiterated in Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana, Chattar
Singh v. State of Haryana, and Krishan Kumar v. State of Haryana, where the Court emphasized
that last seen evidence alone is insufficient, requires corroboration, and cannot be stretched
through conjecture or across wide time gaps. Scientific evidence including DNA analysis,
fingerprints, Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) reports, serology, and ballistics provides objective,
independent verification less prone to human bias. When scientific evidence is neutral or
exculpatory such as DNA mismatches, blood group inconsistencies, or failure to link weapons,
courts cannot ignore these findings and convict on suspicion alone. The fundamental principle,
articulated in Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, mandates that when two views are possible
one indicating guilt and another innocence the accused must receive the benefit of doubt.
Suspicion, regardless of strength, cannot substitute proof beyond reasonable doubt, which remains
the immutable standard in criminal law.

before, saw someone near the crime scene but no TIP was conducted. At trial, Deepak identifies

group creates sufficient corroboration for the dock identification.

options.label: d

The last seen theory principle which requires independent corroboration to establish a

questions.stimulus:
XV. ‘The interpretation of contracts in Indian law follows a structured methodology balancing textual
fidelity with commercial realism. The literal rule serves as the foundational principle, requiring
courts to give contractual terms their plain, grammatical, and ordinary meaning. When language
is clear and unambiguous, courts will not look beyond the text, respecting party autonomy and the
principle of consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). However, the golden rule permits departure
from literal interpretation when it leads to absurd, commercially irrational, or internally
inconsistent outcomes. Courts may adjust meaning sufficiently to avoid absurdity but cannot
rewrite contractual terms to achieve fairness or commercial wisdom.
The purposive approach, borrowed from statutory interpretation, allows courts to examine the
factual matrix and commercial background surrounding the agreement, considering related
documentation, parties' conduct, and the agreement's overall structure. This approach was
articulated in Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd. v. West Bromwich Building Society, where
Lord Hoffmann established that interpretation requires objective understanding as a reasonable
person would have at the time of contracting, considering the matrix of facts available to parties
while excluding prior negotiations and subjective intentions. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The parol evidence rule, codified in Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
restricts use of external evidence to contradict clear written terms, as affirmed in Mangala
Waman Karandikar v. Prakash Damodar Ranade. This ensures the written agreement stands as
the final expression of intent. The doctrine of business efficacy permits courts to imply terms
when essential to ensure contracts deliver their intended commercial result, tested through the
officious bystander test—whether both parties would have agreed with "of course" if the term
had been suggested during negotiations. As applied in Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development
Authority v. Unity Infraprojects Ltd., this doctrine gives practical effect to contracts when written
text insufficiently conveys parties' intention, without rewriting agreements. The contra
proferentem rule resolves persistent ambiguity against the drafting party, particularly in
insurance and consumer contracts or where bargaining power is unequal.
The principle of harmonious construction requires reconciling potentially conflicting
provisions within the same contract, ensuring no clause becomes redundant and the document
operates as an internally coherent whole. Courts also apply what may be termed the principle
against disguise: where parties structure agreements to conceal true commercial nature, courts
examine substance over form, looking beyond surface terminology to reveal actual commercial
effect. This principle reflects the judicial posture that legal consequences flow from substance, not
presentation.
questions.stem:
Alpha Ltd. and Beta Corp. execute a service agreement stating: "Beta shall provide technical
support for 10 lakh monthly." The contract contains no termination clause. After 18 months,
Alpha terminates citing "changed business needs." Beta sues for breach. Alpha argues no
termination clause exists, so either party may exit anytime. Based on the passage, which principle
would most appropriately govern this dispute?

options.label: a
options.text:
The literal rule requiring plain meaning of express terms, under which absence of termination
clause permits unilateral exit

options.label: b
options.text:
The doctrine of business efficacy permitting implication of reasonable notice term to make the
contract commercially workable

options.label: c
options.text:
The parol evidence rule preventing introduction of evidence about parties’ understanding of
termination rights

options.label: d
options.text:
The contra proferentem rule interpreting the ambiguity against Alpha as the party asserting
termination rights

questions.stem:
XYZ Bank's loan agreement with Mohan states: "Borrower shall repay principal with 12% interest
annually. Default triggers penal interest at prevailing market rates." After Mohan defaults, the
Bank charges 24% penal interest (current market rate). Mohan argues "prevailing market rates" is
ambiguous and should mean rates at loan origination (8%). The loan agreement was drafted
entirely by XYZ Bank using its standard format. Based on the passage, which interpretive
principle resolves this ambiguity?

options.label: a
options.text:
The literal rule requiring "prevailing market rates" to mean rates at the time of interpretation,
supporting 24%

options.label: b
options.text:
The golden rule permitting departure from literal meaning because 24% creates commercially
irrational outcome

options.label: c
options.text:
The contra proferentem rule interpreting the ambiguity against XYZ Bank as the drafting
party, favoring 8%

options.label: d
options.text:
The doctrine of business efficacy implying a cap on penal interest to make the contract
commercially reasonable

constituting the foundational mental elements requisite for establishing culpability in most penal
offences. Intention denotes the deliberate purpose or conscious design accompanying the
commission of an act, whereas knowledge signifies cognitive awareness of the probable
consequences emanating from such conduct, notwithstanding the absence of desire for the specific
result. Indian criminal law recognizes a hierarchical gradation of mental states, and this
taxonomy materially influences both the characterization of the offence and the quantum of
liability imposed. The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) distinctly demarcates acts perpetrated
intentionally, knowingly, or with rashness. Culpable homicide as contemplated under Section 299

distinction. When an act is executed with knowledge that harm may potentially ensue, yet
accompanied by subjective optimism that adverse consequences might be averted, penal liability
may nevertheless crystallize. This principle assumes particular salience where the accused
consciously undertook a calculated risk and the deleterious consequence remained objectively
foreseeable. This interpretive framework ensures that criminal liability is not imposed
capriciously or arbitrarily, affirming that the subjective mental state of the accused remains the
analytical fulcrum in determining guilt except where the legislature has expressly displaced this
